How the Studio works, in five short parts. Read this first if anything here is unclear.
Read one card, then go and do that one thing. This room is not meant to be read through in a sitting.

The Carpe Diem’s Forge is where Carpe Diem stops being a finished object and becomes yours. Every word the app says, every course it teaches, and every voice that speaks in it can be rewritten here. Nothing leaves the device: your changes are written where you sit, and they travel only when you carry them yourself.
Open the Studio when the app says something that is not quite true of your work. A single renamed page often does more for the feel of the year than an hour of settings.
How the Studio is laid out

The sidebar on the left holds every room, listed under its shelf name: Start here, How it looks, What it says, The course, Telling people, Sending a copy, and Keeping it safe. Nothing sits behind a strip: scroll the list and every room is there, with the open room marked. The box at the top filters the list as you type.
If you cannot remember which shelf something is on, do not hunt: press the slash key, or open Find, and search for it by name.
The three gestures, and nothing else

Almost everything here works one of three ways. Type in a field to change a word. Empty a field to put the built-in wording back. And where there is a list, restore the whole list to return it as it was made. There is no save button anywhere: a change is kept the moment you leave the field.
If you are unsure whether something took, look at the room’s line in the rail. It counts what you have changed.
Watching the page while you work

Every room offers Show the screen. It puts the part of Carpe Diem that room changes beside your work, and it follows every keystroke. It is the real page, not a drawing of it, so what you see is what a reader sees. In the Tour and the Guidebook there is a second, quieter preview under the fields, which shows the words themselves and says which of them are yours and which are the app’s.
Turn the screen on for anything to do with how the app looks, and off when you are writing long prose, because the movement can pull at your attention.
Making a change you can walk back

Before a large edit, go to Keeping it safe and save a named backup. It takes one press. From then on you can restore that exact state, and restoring keeps what it replaced as its own backup, so even the wrong restore is recoverable. Every single change is also written into a log with the room and the time, and any one of them can be taken back on its own without touching anything else.
The habit worth having: name the backup after what you are about to do, such as “before rewriting the tour”, rather than after the date. You will know which one you want.
Working on one thing at a time

The rooms are small on purpose. A good session is one room, one kind of change, and then a look at the page. If you find yourself with four rooms half-done, that is the moment to stop and save a backup rather than to push on. The change log will still be there tomorrow, and it will tell you exactly where you left off.
When you do not know where to start, start in Checks. It tells you what is worth a second look, and it is a shorter list than your own memory of what needs doing.
Each copy tells its own truth

You send four kinds of copy: your own, the committee demo, the public sample, and the gift edition. The Tour, the Guidebook, and the locks are kept separately for each one, because a reader must not be told about something their copy does not have. Before you send is the room that reads the app itself and lists what that copy will and will not show.
The order that works: author the copy, apply its preset, read Before you send, then make the release. Reading the report last is what stops a copy promising more than it holds.
What a lock can and cannot do

A lock keeps an item off the page. In a single offline file that is all it can do: the words are still inside the file, and anyone who opens the source can read them. If something must genuinely be absent from a copy you send, it has to be left out when the copy is made — which is what a release does, and why the release route exists at all.
Never rely on a lock for anything you would mind being read. Use it for tidiness and for pacing, and use a release for privacy.
When it feels like too much

Thirty rooms is more than anyone holds in mind, and you are not meant to. Nothing here is urgent, nothing is sequential, and nothing breaks if it is left half-done. The Studio remembers the shelf you were on, the room you were in, and every change you made, so you can leave in the middle of a sentence and come back to it. If a room feels heavy, close it: the app underneath is already finished and working.
If you only ever do three things here, let them be these: save a backup before a big edit, keep one room open at a time, and read Before you send before you send.

First empty the field — that alone returns the built-in wording. If a whole room looks wrong, restore its list or, in Keeping it safe, take back the last change. The Carpe Diem’s Forge can build working copies of Carpe Diem for every device you own, in the page, with nothing sent anywhere. The last line of About carries the build: its date, its pass number and a short fingerprint of the file itself. The fingerprint differs between the full app, the demo and the gift on purpose, so two editions can never be mistaken for one another.

Turn writing by hand on or off

Writing by hand puts a small pen beside every field, and lets a pencil write straight onto the page. If you only type, or it gets in the way on a tablet, turn it off here: the pen and the ink stop entirely and typing is left alone. The hand you have taught is kept either way, ready for when you turn it back on.
Off is the quiet choice on a tablet you only type on. Nothing you have taught is lost, and this switch brings it all back.

It shows you a letter, you write it three times on the slate, and it moves on to the next. It remembers where you stopped, so a dozen now and the rest another day is perfectly fine. Write each letter the way you actually write it rather than the way you were taught to, because it is matching your hand and not a copybook. Everything it learns stays on this device.
Do a dozen letters and come back to the rest another day. It always asks for the one it knows least, so nothing is written twice and you never begin again at A.
